clinicalPearls: Classic history is migration of vague, intermittent, crampy epigastric or periumbilical pain to the right lower quadrant over 12-24 h, where it becomes sharper and localizes as transmural inflammation irritates the parietal peritoneum (p.2595).
Maximal tenderness is classically at or near McBurney's point in the right lower quadrant, about one-third of the way along a line from the anterior iliac spine to the umbilicus (p.2596).

Nausea, if present, characteristically follows the onset of abdominal pain (helping distinguish appendicitis from gastroenteritis, in which nausea precedes pain); emesis is typically mild and scant and also occurs after pain onset (p.2595).
Anorexia is so common that the diagnosis of appendicitis should be questioned in its absence (p.2595).
Rovsing's sign: palpation/gentle pressure in the left lower quadrant elicits pain in the right lower quadrant (p.2596).
Iliopsoas sign: extending the right hip causes pain along the posterolateral back and hip, suggesting a retrocecal appendix (p.2596).
Obturator sign: internal rotation of the hip causes pain, suggesting an inflamed appendix located in the pelvis (p.2596).

Patients with appendicitis tend to lie quite still to avoid peritoneal irritation; some report discomfort with a bumpy car ride, coughing, sneezing, or Valsalva-type maneuvers. Parietal peritoneal irritation is often best elicited by gentle percussion, jiggling the bed/gurney, or mildly bumping the feet (p.2596).

Simple appendicitis patients usually appear only mildly ill with pulse and temperature only slightly above normal; temperature >38.3 C (~101 F) or rigors should raise concern for another process or for complications such as perforation, phlegmon, or abscess (p.2596).

Examine the entire abdomen systematically, starting in a non-tender area; all patients should have a rectal examination, and a pelvic examination in women is mandatory to exclude PID, ectopic pregnancy, and ovarian torsion (p.2596).
Appendicitis should be included in the differential diagnosis of abdominal pain for every patient of any age unless it is certain the appendix has been previously removed (p.2595).
harrison.pathophysiology: Etiology is not completely understood. Obstruction of the appendiceal lumen (by fecaliths/appendicoliths, incompletely digested food residue, lymphoid hyperplasia, intraluminal scarring, tumors, bacteria, viruses, or inflammatory bowel disease) is believed, though not proven, to be an important early step at least in some cases. Obstruction leads to bacterial overgrowth and luminal distension with increased intraluminal pressure that can inhibit lymph and blood flow; vascular thrombosis and ischemic necrosis with perforation of the distal appendix may then follow. Perforation near the base of the appendix should raise concern for another disease process. Appendicoliths are found in ~50% of patients with gangrenous appendicitis who perforate but are rarely seen in simpler disease, suggesting differing underlying pathophysiology. Uncomplicated appendicitis does not always progress to perforation; some cases of simple acute appendicitis may temporarily resolve or be managed with antibiotics, though at least one-third will subsequently require appendectomy. When perforation occurs, the leak may be contained by omentum or surrounding tissues to form an abscess, whereas free perforation normally causes severe peritonitis (p.2594-2595).
additionalDifferentials: Ruptured ovarian cyst or other cystic ovarian disease
infectionMimics: Gastroenteritis or colitis (nausea precedes pain, unlike appendicitis) (Harrison 22e p.2595)
Urinary tract infection / genitourinary infection (Harrison 22e p.2596)
In immunocompromised patients: atypical infections from mycobacteria, Cytomegalovirus, or fungi, and neutropenic enterocolitis (Harrison 22e p.2596)
nonInfectiousMimics: Ruptured ovarian cyst / cystic ovarian disease (Harrison 22e p.2595)
additionalInvestigations: WBC count: only mildly to moderately elevated (~10,000-18,000 cells/uL) in ~70% of simple appendicitis; laboratory testing alone does not identify patients with appendicitis (Harrison 22e p.2596).
A left shift toward immature polymorphonuclear leukocytes is present in >95% of cases (Harrison 22e p.2596).
Serum amylase and lipase should be measured; sickle cell preparation may be prudent in patients of African, Spanish, Mediterranean, or Indian ancestry (Harrison 22e p.2596).

Urinalysis to help exclude genitourinary mimics; a few red or white cells may be a nonspecific finding, and an inflamed appendix abutting the ureter or bladder may cause sterile pyuria or hematuria (Harrison 22e p.2596).
Pregnancy test in every woman of childbearing age; cervical cultures if PID is suspected (Harrison 22e p.2596).
Anemia and guaiac-positive stools should raise concern for other disease or complications such as cancer (Harrison 22e p.2596).

Ultrasonography: highly operator dependent; overall sensitivity ~0.86 and specificity ~0.81; appendix may not be visualized even in skilled hands; especially useful (including intravaginal techniques) for pelvic pathology in women. Suggestive findings: wall thickening, increased appendiceal diameter, free fluid (Harrison 22e p.2596).

CT: sensitivity at least 0.94 and specificity at least 0.95; high negative predictive value; suggestive findings include dilatation >6 mm with wall thickening, a lumen that does not fill with enteric contrast, and periappendiceal fatty stranding or air. Presence of luminal air or contrast is NOT consistent with appendicitis; nonvisualization of the appendix is nonspecific and should NOT be used to rule out appendiceal/periappendiceal inflammation (Harrison 22e p.2596).
Plain abdominal films are rarely helpful and not routinely obtained; <5% show an opaque fecalith, and a fecalith is not diagnostic of appendicitis (Harrison 22e p.2596).

For peritonitis: in stable patients with ascites, diagnostic paracentesis is indicated with testing of fluid for protein and LDH and a cell count; radiographs may show bowel dilatation and wall edema, and free air or other leakage may represent a surgical emergency (Harrison 22e p.2597).
redFlags: Free perforation normally causes severe (generalized) peritonitis; perforation risk is ~10-20% and is significantly higher in patients <5 or >65 years of age (Harrison 22e p.2594).
Temperature >38.3 C (~101 F) or rigors suggest a complication (perforation, phlegmon, abscess) or another diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2596).
Persistent symptoms not improved over 48 h are more likely to perforate or develop other complications (Harrison 22e p.2595).
Rare but dreaded complication: infective suppurative thrombosis of the portal vein and its tributaries with intrahepatic abscesses, with very poor prognosis (Harrison 22e p.2595).

Diffuse abdominal tenderness with guarding and rigidity indicates generalized peritonitis; tachycardia, hypotension/volume depletion, significant leukocytosis, and severe acidosis are signs of serious disease (Harrison 22e p.2597).
In pregnancy, perforation raises fetal mortality fourfold (from ~5% to ~20%) (Harrison 22e p.2596).
Postoperative fever and leukocytosis persisting beyond 5 days should raise concern for an intraabdominal abscess (Harrison 22e p.2597).
harrison.prognosis: Mortality from simple appendicitis is currently <1%, and for uncomplicated nonperforated appendicitis the operative mortality rate is 0.1-0.5% (approximating the risk of general anesthesia). Mortality for perforated or otherwise complicated disease is much higher, ranging from ~3% overall to as high as 15% in the elderly. For acute peritonitis, mortality can be <10% in reasonably healthy patients with relatively uncomplicated, localized disease but >40% in the elderly or immunocompromised (Harrison 22e p.2597).
pitfalls: Atypical presentations and pain patterns are common, especially in the very old and very young; signs and symptoms can be subtle in the elderly, who may not react vigorously, with nausea/anorexia/emesis predominating (Harrison 22e p.2596).

Retrocecal or pelvic (below the pelvic brim) appendix may prompt very little anterior abdominal wall tenderness; pelvic appendicitis may present with dysuria, urinary frequency, diarrhea, or tenesmus and only suprapubic or rectal/pelvic-exam tenderness (Harrison 22e p.2596).

Appendiceal location varies widely (right lower quadrant, pelvis, right flank, right upper quadrant, or even the left side with malrotation/redundant colon), influencing presentation; delay in diagnosis is more likely when the appendix is unusually positioned (Harrison 22e p.2595).

Diagnosing appendicitis in children is challenging (dramatic response to stimulation, difficult history); the smaller pediatric omentum may be less able to wall off a perforation (Harrison 22e p.2596).

Pregnancy: appendicitis is the most common extrauterine general surgical emergency in pregnancy; early symptoms (nausea, anorexia) may be overlooked and the enlarging/gravid uterus may displace the appendix higher and obscure typical findings (Harrison 22e p.2596).
Immunocompromised patients may present with only mild tenderness; do not be overly cautious and delay operation in those believed to have appendicitis (Harrison 22e p.2596).
Laboratory testing alone does not identify appendicitis, and no currently available decision tool obviates the need for expert clinical opinion (Harrison 22e p.2596).
A fecalith is not diagnostic of appendicitis, though its presence in an appropriate location with pain is suggestive and associated with greater likelihood of complications (Harrison 22e p.2596).
harrison.severityClassification: No formal grading scale is presented; disease is broadly distinguished as simple/uncomplicated appendicitis (without gangrenous necrosis, appendicoliths, perforation, or tumors) versus complicated disease (gangrene, perforation, phlegmon, abscess). Peritonitis is classified as secondary (most commonly from perforation of a hollow viscus, e.g., appendix, colonic diverticula, stomach/duodenum) versus primary or spontaneous (no identifiable intraabdominal source; >90% occur in patients with ascites or hypoproteinemia <1 g/L), and either type may be localized or diffuse; aseptic/chemical peritonitis (e.g., from gastric juice, bile, pancreatic enzymes, blood, or urine) is also distinguished (Harrison 22e p.2595-2597).
management: Appendicectomy, laparoscopic where feasible, as definitive treatment for uncomplicated appendicitis
Perioperative intravenous antibiotics, with broad-spectrum cover and resuscitation for perforation or peritonitis
Preoperative resuscitation with intravenous fluids, analgesia, antiemetics and nil by mouth
Non-operative antibiotic management as a selected option in uncomplicated cases or where surgery is contraindicated
Percutaneous drainage of a well-formed appendiceal abscess, with interval appendicectomy considered
Source control with peritoneal washout at operation for generalised peritonitis, and postoperative critical care if septic
Histological examination of the specimen, with consideration of underlying malignancy when the appendiceal base is involved
